network.overall_strategy: The supplied literature does not establish ten mechanistically independent, experimentally closed prebiotic syntheses of isoleucine. This network therefore distinguishes ten feedstock- or catalyst-resolved pathway variants: seven experimentally studied hydrocarbon-discharge entries followed by inferred Strecker chemistry, and three experimentally supported reductive-amination variants conditional on supplied 3-methyl-2-oxopentanoic acid. The latter precursor has no demonstrated prebiotic source in the supplied evidence. Discharge reactions are lumped, target-directed channels: amino-acid detection is established, but production and isolation of the proposed 2-methylbutanal intermediate are not. Natural hydrolysis conditions are distinguished from the harsher analytical work-up used to identify discharge products. No pathway selectively produces L-isoleucine; the target is accompanied by D-isoleucine and allo-isoleucine stereoisomers. Unspecified-stereochemistry precursor nodes represent unresolved stereoisomer inventories, not purified compounds. Neutral molecular formulas are used for acid-base families, with protonation and counterions described in conditions. Starting species may also appear as coproducts; independent hydrogen supply is assumed for catalytic pathways, not transfer from discharge experiments. Formation-environment labels identify a representative setting; reaction nodes specify alternative settings. Terminal coproducts use the permitted intermediate role because the schema has no byproduct role. All settings are anoxic. Strong surface UV is an additional degradation constraint, not an assumed selective synthesis mechanism.

molecules.common_name: Alpha-keto-beta-methylvaleric acid; supplied precursor with unspecified stereochemistry

reactions.name: Methane-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.temperature: Approximately 300 K bulk water; published benchmark approximately 298 K
conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric experimental gas mixture; methane benchmark approximately 300 torr CH4 and 80 torr N2
conditions.other: Electrical discharge above an anoxic aqueous reservoir near pH 8.7; benchmark used 48 h discharge followed by 48 h standing. Plasma temperatures are not the bulk-water temperature. N2 and ammonia represent available nitrogen reservoirs; nitrogen-source partitioning is unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped radical fragmentation, carbon-chain assembly and water-derived oxygen incorporation generate a mixed carbonyl inventory and cyanide. Formation of the particular 2-methylbutanal channel is inferred from a Strecker interpretation, not resolved as an elementary sequence. H2 represents a possible net dehydrogenation coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Methane-discharge products yielded isoleucine and allo-isoleucine after analytical hydrolysis: approximately 0.7 and 0.5 mol per 100 mol glycine, respectively (Ring et al., 1972; Ring and Miller, 1984). These are amino-acid inventory ratios, not aldehyde yields. The specific 2-methylbutanal output is an inferred, unverified intermediate assignment. This unresolved, low-selectivity branched-skeleton assembly is the principal bottleneck. A locally reducing atmosphere is required; relevance to a predominantly CO2/N2 atmosphere is uncertain.

reactions.name: Ethane-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric reducing gas mixture; feed-specific partial pressures not verified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Ethane/N2/ammonia/water discharge system; aqueous reservoir near pH 8.7. Electrical discharge supplies energy without molecular oxygen.

reactions.mechanism: Ethane-derived radicals undergo fragmentation and recombination, producing a broad organic inventory. The graph resolves only the inferred 2-methylbutanal/cyanide channel relevant to subsequent Strecker chemistry.
reactions.reasoning: Ethane experiments gave approximately 1.1 mol isoleucine and 1.4 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine after hydrolysis (Ring and Miller, 1984). This supports a distinct experimentally tested feedstock variant, not a distinct established elementary mechanism. Isolation or selective formation of 2-methylbutanal was not established in the supplied evidence; its placement here is a mechanistic inference.

reactions.name: Ethene-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric reducing gas mixture; feed-specific partial pressures not verified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Ethene/N2/ammonia/water exposed to electrical discharge; aqueous collection near pH 8.7; no O2.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-generated radicals add to and fragment ethene, followed by nonselective chain growth and formation of nitrogenous and oxygenated products. The branched aldehyde is an inferred member of this unresolved inventory.
reactions.reasoning: Ethene discharge yielded approximately 1.2 mol isoleucine and 1.5 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine after hydrolysis (Ring and Miller, 1984). No preferential formation of the proteinogenic stereoisomer follows from these observations. The carbonyl-specific edge remains inferred rather than directly demonstrated, and the geological abundance of ethene-rich gas mixtures is an additional constraint.

reactions.name: Ethyne-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric reducing gas mixture; feed-specific partial pressures not verified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Ethyne/N2/ammonia/water discharge; aqueous collection near pH 8.7. Competing polymerization and formation of numerous unrelated products are expected.

reactions.mechanism: Energetic radical addition and fragmentation involving ethyne build a heterogeneous carbon inventory. Water-derived reactive species introduce oxygen; nitrogen activation generates cyanide. The required branched C5 aldehyde channel remains unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: The reported hydrolysate contained approximately 3.2 mol isoleucine and 3.1 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine (Ring and Miller, 1984). These relative values do not establish a high absolute carbon yield or selective aldehyde synthesis. Formation of 2-methylbutanal is an explicitly inferred intermediate assignment; an ethyne supply and preservation of products under surface irradiation remain geochemical limitations.

reactions.name: Propane-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric reducing gas mixture; feed-specific partial pressures not verified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Propane/N2/ammonia/water discharge with aqueous collection near pH 8.7; no molecular oxygen.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen abstraction, fragmentation and radical recombination produce mixed carbonyl and cyanide precursors. The graph shows the inferred low-flux channel toward 2-methylbutanal rather than an established selective transformation of propane.
reactions.reasoning: Propane gave approximately 0.17 mol isoleucine and 0.22 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine after hydrolysis, among the lower relative yields in the tested series (Ring and Miller, 1984). It is retained because it is an experimentally tested alternative, not because it is efficient. The proposed aldehyde intermediate and its individual yield remain unverified.

reactions.name: n-Butane-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric reducing gas mixture; feed-specific partial pressures not verified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Butane/N2/ammonia/water discharge; aqueous collection near pH 8.7. The feedstock is not assumed to undergo clean one-carbon homologation.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-driven hydrogen abstraction and radical recombination generate ketones, aldehydes and other products. Access to the required branched C5 aldehyde involves unresolved carbon assembly rather than simple oxidation of butane.
reactions.reasoning: Butane experiments yielded approximately 4.1 mol isoleucine and 3.6 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine after hydrolysis (Ring and Miller, 1984). The relatively large ratios do not demonstrate efficient or selective synthesis. Secondary-site oxidation of butane can instead favor butanone and an isovaline-related channel; the 2-methylbutanal assignment here is an inference from the final product inventory, not a documented selective route.

reactions.name: Isobutane-discharge entry to the inferred branched-aldehyde and cyanide pool

conditions.pressure: Subatmospheric reducing gas mixture; feed-specific partial pressures not verified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Isobutane/N2/ammonia/water discharge and aqueous collection near pH 8.7. Fragmentation and recombination are required; preservation of the initial branching pattern is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: A nonselective radical network fragments and recombines the branched hydrocarbon. The proposed sec-butyl-bearing aldehyde channel is embedded in a much larger inventory, including competing valine-related precursors.
reactions.reasoning: Isobutane experiments gave approximately 3.3 mol isoleucine and 3.2 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine after hydrolysis (Ring and Miller, 1984). The same study strongly favored valine under this feed, so starting with a branched hydrocarbon does not selectively solve isoleucine skeleton assembly. The 2-methylbutanal output is inferred and not independently verified.

reactions.name: Reversible imine formation from the branched aldehyde

conditions.other: Mildly alkaline, ammonia-containing collected solution, approximately pH 8-9. Imine need not accumulate or be isolated; subsequent cyanide trapping can capture its equilibrium population.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde to form a transient carbinolamine, followed by reversible dehydration to an imine or its protonated form.
reactions.reasoning: This is the conventional mechanistic entry to Strecker aminonitrile formation. Ring and Miller (1984) discuss increased aminonitrile formation relative to hydroxynitriles at higher ammonia availability. The reaction class is well established, but isolation of this particular imine under the reported prebiotic conditions was not supplied; its explicit node is a mechanistic inference. This step installs nitrogen but does not solve the upstream branched-skeleton problem.

reactions.name: Strecker cyanide capture of the branched imine

conditions.other: Aqueous HCN/CN- and ammonia near pH 8-9; no chiral catalyst or resolving agent. HCN volatilization, photochemical loss and competing cyanohydrin formation can reduce productive flux.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine/iminium carbon, followed by proton transfer, creating the future amino-acid alpha stereocenter. A racemic branched aldehyde precursor gives an unresolved aminonitrile stereoisomer inventory.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker chemistry provides a chemically supported interpretation of the discharge amino-acid inventory (Ring et al., 1972; Ring and Miller, 1984). Patel et al. (2015) independently demonstrate related prebiotic aminonitrile chemistry, but their cyanosulfidic network does not establish this isoleucine precursor. Application to the inferred 2-methylbutanal inventory is therefore a substrate-specific mechanistic inference, not an independently demonstrated selective route.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile hydrolysis to the isoleucine and allo-isoleucine inventory
agents: Hydronium ions as general acid catalysts

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K for the proposed geothermal-pool analogue
conditions.other: Proposed acidic geothermal episode, approximately pH 1-3, with sustained liquid water. Required residence time and conversion are unmeasured for this precursor. The analytical benchmark instead used 3 M HCl at approximately 378 K for 24 h. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium under acidic conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration produces an intermediate amide, followed by amide hydrolysis to the amino acid and ammonia/ammonium. The four product nodes represent an unresolved stereoisomer inventory, not stereochemical purification.
reactions.reasoning: Isoleucine and allo-isoleucine were identified after strong-acid hydrolysis of discharge products (Ring et al., 1972; Ring and Miller, 1984). Hydrolysis is established chemistry, but conversion at the milder proposed natural conditions is an unvalidated extrapolation and a kinetic bottleneck. The published work-up does not demonstrate comparable accumulation of free amino acids in an ambient pool. Approximately comparable Ile and allo-Ile inventories and racemic products preclude an L-isoleucine selectivity claim.

reactions.name: Supported-nickel hydrogenative amination of supplied branched keto acid
agents: Nickel supported on silica-alumina; laboratory catalyst benchmark

conditions.other: 30 mM supplied keto acid, approximately 150 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8, 72 h. Classified as a low-temperature mineral-interface analogue, not a 350-600 K hydrothermal experiment. Independent H2 supply is required.

reactions.mechanism: The keto group condenses reversibly with ammonia, and nickel activates hydrogen to reduce the resulting imine/iminium. Direct carbonyl hydrogenation competes through rxn_014.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated amination of supplied alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate under these conditions. The reported 6-84% combined amino/hydroxy-acid yields for Ni or meteorite catalysts span several substrates and must not be assigned as an isoleucine-specific yield. Amino and hydroxy products were often roughly comparable. The supported catalyst is an experimental surrogate, not a demonstrated natural assemblage. The four amino-acid stereoisomers are expected from racemic precursor and nonselective amination, but their individual distribution was not verified in the supplied report. No upstream prebiotic keto-acid synthesis is established.

reactions.name: Palladium hydrogenative amination of supplied branched keto acid
agents: Palladium on carbon; laboratory catalyst benchmark

conditions.other: 30 mM supplied keto acid, approximately 150 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8, 72 h. Pd abundance and access to suitable catalytic surfaces are major geological limitations.

reactions.mechanism: Palladium-catalyzed hydrogen activation reduces the ammonia-derived imine/iminium. Direct ketone reduction remains a competing branch through rxn_015.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated the reductive-amination reaction class, including the isoleucine keto-acid precursor, with Pd/C. Across the reported substrate panel, Pd generally favored amino acids more strongly than Ni or meteorite catalysts; the panel-wide 52-88% yields and usually greater than 5:1 amino/hydroxy selectivity are not asserted as this substrate's values. This is an experimentally justified comparator but a lower-geochemical-plausibility variant because Pd is rare and Pd/C is an engineered material. Keto-acid availability and stereoisomer selection remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Meteoritic-metal hydrogenative amination of supplied branched keto acid
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite containing Fe-Ni metal

conditions.catalyst: Ground Aletai meteorite; reported benchmark approximately 3 mg and 18 mol% Ni
conditions.other: 30 mM supplied keto acid, approximately 150 mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8, 72 h. Requires accessible reduced metal surfaces; weathering, passivation and sulfur poisoning can alter activity.

reactions.mechanism: Accessible meteoritic metal surfaces activate hydrogen and reduce ammonia-derived imine intermediates. Carbonyl reduction competes through rxn_016.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated keto-acid reduction and amination using ground Aletai meteorite. This provides a natural-material catalyst benchmark, but experimentally ground metal is not equivalent to an arbitrary meteorite surface in a pool. Competing hydroxy-acid production is substantial. Formation of all four amino-acid stereoisomers is an expectation rather than a verified stereochemical measurement in the supplied account. The precursor was supplied, so the experiment does not close a de novo prebiotic pathway to isoleucine.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-catalyzed reduction to the branched hydroxy acid

conditions.other: Same pH 8, ammonium-bicarbonate-containing reaction mixture as rxn_011; approximately 72 h. This branch competes for the supplied keto acid.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-activated hydrogen reduces the keto carbonyl directly to a secondary alcohol without nitrogen incorporation.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) report corresponding alpha-hydroxy acids alongside amino acids, with approximately comparable amino/hydroxy production frequently observed for Ni and meteorite catalysts. This competing sink is included rather than representing all keto-acid consumption as productive isoleucine synthesis. No conversion of this hydroxy acid back into a productive precursor is assumed.

reactions.name: Competing palladium-catalyzed reduction to the branched hydroxy acid

conditions.other: Same pH 8, ammonium-bicarbonate-containing mixture as rxn_012; approximately 72 h. Relative flux is substrate- and catalyst-dependent.

reactions.mechanism: Direct catalytic hydrogenation of the keto group forms the corresponding hydroxy acid, bypassing imine formation.
reactions.reasoning: Hydroxy-acid formation competes with Pd-mediated reductive amination, although Pd generally favors amino-acid formation more strongly than the Ni and meteorite systems in the reported substrate panel (Kaur et al., 2024). No substrate-specific numerical branching ratio is assigned because it was not verified in the supplied findings.

reactions.name: Competing meteoritic-metal reduction to the branched hydroxy acid
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite containing Fe-Ni metal

conditions.other: Same pH 8, ammonium-bicarbonate-containing mixture and approximately 72 h exposure as rxn_013. Reduced, accessible metal surface is necessary.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen activated on meteoritic metal reduces the carbonyl directly, producing an unresolved hydroxy-acid stereoisomer inventory.
reactions.reasoning: The meteorite-catalyzed experiments produced hydroxy acids as substantial competing products rather than selectively aminating all supplied keto acid (Kaur et al., 2024). Including this branch captures an experimentally supported limitation. Natural surface passivation and uncertain precursor supply further restrict geological extrapolation.

pathways.name: Methane-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: C1 feedstock entry with demonstrated isoleucine detection after laboratory hydrolysis. The specific branched-aldehyde and imine assignments are inferred, and the proposed milder natural hydrolysis conditions remain unvalidated. Produces a racemic Ile/allo-Ile inventory.

pathways.name: Ethane-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: Experimentally tested ethane entry into the same inferred Strecker mechanism. Distinct by hydrocarbon feedstock, not by an independently established downstream mechanism. Shares the unresolved aldehyde assignment and natural-hydrolysis limitations of P1.

pathways.name: Ethene-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: Experimentally tested unsaturated C2 feedstock entry. Hydrolysate identification supports nonselective target formation, not selective branched-aldehyde synthesis or L-isoleucine enrichment.

pathways.name: Ethyne-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: Experimentally tested acetylene entry with relatively elevated Ile/glycine ratios, but no established absolute efficiency or stereoselectivity. The carbon-assembly mechanism and natural precursor hydrolysis remain incompletely demonstrated.

pathways.name: Propane-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: Experimentally tested low-relative-yield propane entry. Retained as an observed feedstock alternative without implying efficient carbon-skeleton construction or selective target accumulation.

pathways.name: n-Butane-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: Experimentally tested C4 feedstock entry. The observed Ile/allo-Ile products do not establish direct or selective homologation of butane to 2-methylbutanal; this skeleton-forming portion remains unresolved.

pathways.name: Isobutane-discharge/Strecker pathway variant
pathways.description: Experimentally tested branched-hydrocarbon entry. Radical scrambling permits a minor isoleucine precursor inventory, but the starting branching pattern does not selectively determine the target skeleton.

pathways.name: Conditional supported-nickel reductive-amination pathway
pathways.description: Demonstrated precursor-to-amino-acid transformation conditional on supplied 3-methyl-2-oxopentanoic acid. This is not a closed synthesis from simple prebiotic feedstocks. Competing rxn_014 diverts precursor to hydroxy acid. Catalyst-defined variant of the same reaction family as P9 and P10.

pathways.name: Conditional palladium reductive-amination pathway
pathways.description: Experimentally supported catalytic comparator beginning with supplied branched keto acid. Geological Pd availability and the engineered support make it less compelling as a natural route. Competing rxn_015 remains active; no stereoisomer selection or upstream keto-acid synthesis is established.

pathways.name: Conditional meteoritic-metal reductive-amination pathway
pathways.description: Natural-material catalyst benchmark beginning with supplied branched keto acid and independent H2. It does not demonstrate meteoritic or terrestrial synthesis of that precursor. Competing rxn_016 consumes the same precursor; accessibility of fresh metal and stereochemical selection remain limitations.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring & Miller (1984) support methane-discharge production of isoleucine and allo-isoleucine after analytical hydrolysis, reporting approximately 0.7 and 0.5 mol per 100 mol glycine, respectively. This supports the overall product assignment but does not experimentally establish the specific 2-methylbutanal channel in rxn_001. The subsequent Strecker chemistry is plausible. Although the strategy distinguishes natural hydrolysis from analytical work-up, rxn_010 supplies no natural pH, temperature, residence time or conversion evidence. All reactions pass the supplied conservation check.
suggestions: Attach reaction-local citations and specify methane and nitrogen partial pressures, ammonia concentration, discharge exposure and aqueous collection conditions.
Measure mol_013 or establish its involvement through isotope tracing; isolation is not necessary if in situ formation and conversion can be demonstrated.
Specify and validate natural hydrolysis conditions separately from the cited 3 M HCl, 105 degrees C, 24-hour analytical work-up.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Ring & Miller (1984) results support ethane-discharge isoleucine and allo-isoleucine detection at approximately 1.1 and 1.4 mol per 100 mol glycine. The proposed aldehyde intermediate remains inferred rather than identified. Consequently, this is a plausible interpretation of experimentally observed products, not an experimentally resolved sequence through mol_013 and mol_015. Natural completion of rxn_010 remains insufficiently specified. Formation of L-isoleucine within a stereoisomer mixture counts toward target achievement.
suggestions: Provide ethane-specific experimental conditions and evidence connecting the discharge mixture to the proposed branched aldehyde or aminonitrile.
Document aqueous capture, reactant concentrations and ammonia-dependent aminonitrile formation.
Establish hydrolysis rates and product survival under an explicitly stated natural surface regime.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ethylene-discharge experiments reported approximately 1.2 mol isoleucine and 1.5 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine in Ring & Miller (1984). These observations support nonselective target production after work-up, but not the precise carbon-skeleton-building chemistry encoded in rxn_003. Imine formation and cyanide capture are chemically reasonable conditional on an available aldehyde pool. The unspecified surface conditions and unvalidated natural aminonitrile hydrolysis limit confidence in the complete environmental pathway.
suggestions: Add ethylene-specific gas composition, discharge duration, aqueous pH and intermediate measurements.
Keep rxn_003 explicitly marked as a lumped, inferred channel rather than an experimentally established aldehyde synthesis.
Demonstrate conversion of the resulting aminonitrile inventory to free amino acids without relying solely on analytical acid hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring & Miller (1984) reported approximately 3.2 mol isoleucine and 3.1 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine from acetylene discharge. These relative abundances establish product occurrence but are neither absolute carbon yields nor evidence for selective 2-methylbutanal formation. The inferred coefficients for rxn_004 satisfy conservation and are not a demonstrated product distribution. The main unresolved links remain the specific aldehyde-producing channel and environmentally effective hydrolysis.
suggestions: Separate the mathematical balance of rxn_004 from experimentally measured carbon flux and product yields.
Provide acetylene-discharge conditions and evidence for formation or consumption of mol_013.
Specify hydrolysis conditions and competing degradation rates under the proposed surface exposure.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied propane-discharge results report approximately 0.17 mol isoleucine and 0.22 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine. This supports low-abundance product formation, not absence of a route. No additional penalty is assigned simply for the feedstock or its lower reported relative yield. As in the other discharge variants, the specific branched-aldehyde intermediate is unverified, and free-amino-acid production under the stated natural environment is not established by the analytical hydrolysis result alone.
suggestions: Report absolute yields, precursor concentrations and analytical identification supporting the proposed propane-derived intermediate inventory.
Specify discharge-to-water collection conditions and residence times for Strecker chemistry.
Demonstrate natural hydrolysis and amino-acid persistence at the concentrations actually generated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The n-butane experiments reported approximately 4.1 mol isoleucine and 3.6 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine. These are strong evidence for product occurrence within a complex discharge mixture, but they do not identify the proposed C5 aldehyde. The literature also discusses butanone formation from butane oxidation; that different carbonyl does not establish mol_013. Downstream Strecker chemistry is sound in principle, while the natural hydrolysis regime remains unspecified.
suggestions: Distinguish 2-methylbutanal experimentally from butanone and other carbonyl products rather than inferring its identity solely from amino-acid detection.
Add feed-specific discharge conditions and reaction-local Ring & Miller citations.
Provide a validated environmental hydrolysis step with temperature, pH, duration and conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Isobutane-discharge experiments reported approximately 3.3 mol isoleucine and 3.2 mol allo-isoleucine per 100 mol glycine. This supports the target-containing product inventory. Evidence discussed for isobutyraldehyde and valine formation from isobutane does not directly establish the structurally different 2-methylbutanal intermediate required here. The proposed sequence is chemically plausible but experimentally unresolved upstream, with an additional environmental completion gap at rxn_010.
suggestions: Verify the identity and availability of the C5 branched aldehyde without substituting evidence for isobutyraldehyde formation.
Specify isobutane-discharge conditions, aqueous collection and ammonia availability.
Demonstrate aminonitrile hydrolysis under a stated natural regime and distinguish measured stereoisomer ratios from inventory bookkeeping.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) support hydrogenative amination of supplied alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate using supported nickel, and rxn_014 appropriately represents competing hydroxy-acid formation. The transformation is chemically strong conditional on the supplied substrate. Its missing prebiotic source limits environmental self-sufficiency, not the validity of the substrate-to-product reaction. The label 'Biochemical' does not specify an environment, and laboratory Ni/SiO2-Al2O3 cannot automatically be equated with an available natural catalyst. Exact four-stereoisomer yields are not established by the supplied study summary.
suggestions: Attach the Kaur et al. citation and explicit benchmark conditions: 22 degrees C, pH 8, 5 bar H2, 72 hours, ammonium bicarbonate and supported-nickel loading.
Justify the presence and activity of the proposed supported catalyst or experimentally validate a specific natural analogue.
Retain mol_020 as an external dependency unless an evidence-based source is supplied, and quantify substrate-specific amino-acid versus hydroxy-acid branching.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Kaur et al. (2024) findings strongly support Pd/C-catalyzed reductive amination of the supplied keto acid and support retaining a competing hydroxy-acid branch. Higher amino-acid selectivity reported across the substrate set should not be treated as an exact isoleucine-specific yield. Environmental confidence is limited by the absence of a specified accessible, active palladium catalyst and reaction conditions, not by any intrinsic objection to palladium chemistry. The starting keto-acid dependency remains explicit and unresolved.
suggestions: Specify Pd/C or another experimentally validated catalyst rather than generic palladium, including catalyst loading and support.
Identify a physically credible source and concentration of active palladium in the proposed setting; geological rarity alone neither proves nor rules out availability.
Provide hydrogen activity, ammonia concentration, pH, temperature and reaction duration, together with keto-acid-specific yields and stereochemical analysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest conditional pathway because the supplied Kaur et al. (2024) study directly tested a naturally occurring meteoritic-metal catalyst, supporting both amino-acid formation and competing hydroxy-acid production. Independent hydrogen supply is explicitly assumed, so transfer of discharge-generated H2 is not required. Nevertheless, catalyst exposure and activity, hydrogen conditions and the source of mol_020 remain unestablished for the proposed environment. Approval at the pathway threshold applies only to conversion of the supplied precursor, not to a demonstrated self-contained prebiotic synthesis.
suggestions: Specify the tested meteorite material, metal loading, exposed surface state and hydrogen activity, using the Kaur et al. benchmark conditions explicitly.
Justify co-location of active metal, supplied keto acid, ammonia and independently supplied H2, and evaluate catalyst passivation.
Keep precursor availability conditional and measure substrate-specific amino/hydroxy product yields and stereoisomer distributions.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid: all 21 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes belong to one connected component, molecule IDs are consistent, and the supplied deterministic check establishes five reactions balanced as written and eleven balanceable with coefficients. There are no conservation violations. Mathematical coefficients for the four stereoisomer products do not establish equal experimental yields. Scores for rxn_014 through rxn_016 cover the competing branches associated with P8 through P10, not additional target-forming steps. Literature alignment is good in its explicit acknowledgment of inferred discharge intermediates, supplied keto-acid dependence, analytical work-up, competing reduction and unresolved stereochemistry. However, explicit citations and numerical conditions are absent from the submitted reaction descriptions. The principal network-level gaps are experimental support for the specific mol_013-producing channels in rxn_001 through rxn_007 and an environmentally validated hydrolysis regime for rxn_010. The catalytic branches establish credible supplied-substrate conversions, but not a demonstrated natural source of mol_020. Surface/Biochemical labels and anoxia alone are insufficient to verify pH, temperature, pressure, reactant activities and catalyst availability. No transfer from discharge-generated hydrogen to catalytic settings is assumed or required. Production of L-isoleucine within a mixture counts toward the stated target; lack of enantiopurity is not itself a failure, although exact stereoisomer distributions remain unverified. Neither the number of pathway variants nor their shared intermediates affects the score. Overall, this is a credible, candidly qualified synthesis hypothesis with supported endpoint chemistry, but not an experimentally closed natural synthesis network. It is not approved at the 0.90 network threshold.
